client: Lately, I’ve been feeling so much pressure to keep my GPA perfect, especially after getting a C in calculus last semester. I keep worrying that one bad grade is going to ruin everything, and I’m scared I won’t be able to catch up or meet expectations. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like the pressure is just part of college life, and I don’t know if there’s a way to make it better.
therapist: It sounds like that C in calculus has really shaken your confidence, and you're carrying a heavy weight of expectations about what it means for your future. I hear how overwhelming it feels when you tell yourself that one grade could ruin everything—that kind of thinking would make anyone anxious. What do you think might happen if you explored whether that belief is 100% true?

client: I guess I know logically that one C won't ruin everything, but it feels like I'm falling behind all my classmates who seem to have perfect grades. My parents always emphasized how important grades are for getting into grad school, so it's hard not to see this as some huge failure. I don't know how to stop feeling like I've already messed everything up.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel this way when comparing yourself to others and carrying your parents' expectations—that's a lot of pressure to hold. I notice you're able to recognize this thought isn't completely logical, even though it feels true emotionally—that's a really important awareness. What would it be like to gently challenge the idea that your worth or future depends on any single grade?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to separate my worth from my grades when they've always been how I measure success. Like, if I don't have perfect grades, what else do I have? I've built my whole identity around being a good student, so this feels really shaky. Maybe that sounds dramatic, but that's honestly how it feels.
therapist: You're describing something really profound—how your sense of self has become so tied to academic achievement that any imperfection feels like losing part of who you are. That doesn't sound dramatic at all; it sounds like a deeply ingrained belief that's served a purpose but might be limiting you now. What might it look like to start exploring other parts of yourself beyond being a student?

client: I've never really thought about myself outside of academics before. The idea is kind of scary because I don't even know what else I'd focus on. But also... I do remember loving photography in high school before college got so intense. I just don't see how that could be as important as keeping my grades up.
therapist: It sounds like photography was something that brought you joy, but it got pushed aside when academics took center stage—that happens so often when we’re trying to meet high expectations. I wonder if there’s a way to explore photography again, even in small doses, to reconnect with that sense of joy and creativity. What do you think might happen if you allowed yourself to prioritize something enjoyable, even alongside your studies?

client: I guess I could try taking some photos on weekends, but I worry it would feel like wasting time I should spend studying. The guilt would probably ruin any enjoyment. Plus, what if I discover I'm not even good at photography anymore? Then I'd just feel like a failure at that too.
therapist: It sounds like even considering something enjoyable brings up guilt and fear of failure—like there's no room for imperfection in any area of your life. That must feel exhausting, carrying all these "what ifs" about both academics and hobbies. What would it be like to experiment with photography just as an act of self-care, without any pressure to be "good" at it?

client: That actually sounds kind of terrifying—doing something just for me without any goal or standard to meet. I've never really thought about self-care that way before. But I also wonder if I'd just feel restless the whole time, like I should be doing something more productive instead. It's hard to imagine letting myself just enjoy something without judging it.
therapist: It makes sense that this feels terrifying—it’s a big shift from how you’ve approached life so far, where everything seems to need a purpose or a standard to meet. That restlessness you’re describing might be part of unlearning the belief that your worth depends on productivity. What would it be like to start small, maybe just 10 minutes with your camera, and notice what comes up without needing to judge or fix it?

client: I guess I could try 10 minutes, but I’m pretty sure I’d spend the whole time thinking about all the assignments I should be doing instead. It’s hard to imagine actually enjoying something without feeling guilty about it. What if I end up just feeling more stressed because I’m “wasting” time?
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of trying something for yourself brings up a lot of guilt and worry about falling behind—it’s like your mind is constantly reminding you of all the “shoulds.” That’s a really common response when we’re used to prioritizing productivity over everything else. What would it be like to notice those thoughts as just thoughts, rather than facts, and still give yourself permission to try?

client: I can see what you're saying about thoughts not being facts, but that feels so abstract when the anxiety is so real. Even when I try to notice the thoughts, they still feel urgent and true in the moment. Maybe I need some concrete way to challenge them, but I don't know how to do that when the pressure feels so overwhelming.
therapist: It’s completely valid that the anxiety feels so real and urgent—it’s designed to grab your attention, even when the thoughts behind it might not reflect reality. One concrete way to challenge them could be to write down the specific thoughts that come up, like “I’m falling behind” or “This will ruin everything,” and then gently ask yourself what evidence supports or contradicts them. How might it feel to try that the next time the pressure feels overwhelming?

client: Writing down the thoughts sounds like it could help, but I worry I won’t be able to see them clearly when I’m in the middle of feeling anxious. It’s like everything just spirals, and I can’t think rationally enough to question anything. What if I just end up fueling the anxiety more by focusing on those thoughts?
therapist: That's a really understandable concern—when anxiety takes over, it can feel impossible to step back and examine thoughts objectively. Maybe we could start by having you jot them down after the anxiety peaks, when the intensity has settled a bit, so it feels less overwhelming. How does that idea land with you?

client: That might work better—at least I wouldn’t feel like I have to fight the anxiety in the moment. But I still worry that by the time the anxiety passes, I’ll just want to forget about it and move on. Writing things down after the fact feels like reopening a wound I’d rather leave alone.
therapist: It makes sense that revisiting those anxious moments later might feel like picking at something painful—that protective instinct to avoid discomfort is completely natural. At the same time, I wonder if gently exploring those thoughts when you're calmer could actually help reduce their power over time, like airing out a wound so it heals better. What do you imagine might happen if you tried this just once, keeping it brief and kind with yourself?
